newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK PM REJECTS COMBINED NATO/PRESIDENT REFENDUM.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK PM REJECTS COMBINED NATO/PRESIDENT REFENDUM.

text.p: Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar rejected on Monday the possible combination of a referendum on direct presidential elections with a referendum on the country's possible entry into NATO.
"I have found it unreasonable to link this (NATO referendum) with the question of direct vote on the president," Meciar told Slovak Radio. "These (two) things are unequal and unbalanced."
Meciar's ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) spearheaded a campaign for a referendum on the country's possible entry into NATO. Earlier this month parliament approved such a vote.
Meanwhile, Slovakia's opposition said it had collected more than 350,000 signatures needed to force a referendum on the direct election of the President.
The petitioners have said they would like the referendum on presidential elections to be held on the same day as the NATO plebiscite.
But Meciar, an avowed political foe of President Michal Kovac, has rejected the referendum on direct presidential elections calling on voters to boycott the move.
"It (the combination of both referenda) can be only an attempt to make people to attend this (presidential) referendum," he said.

The governing coalition, led by HZDS, and the opposition appear unable to agree on a common presidential candidate and neither is able to garner the three-fifths majority necessary in the 150-seat house to push through their own choice in a vote shceduled for March 1998.

If such a stalemate occurs, Meciar would assume presidential powers until a new parliament is elected at elections planned for the autumn of 1998, when the body would again have to propose a presidential candidate.

Under Slovak law, if a petition has 350,000 signatures, the president must call a referendum on the subject within 90 days of receiving the request from those who have collected the signatures. However, it is fully in hands of Kovac to decide on the dates of both the referenda.
Meciar hinted that his government would ask the country's Constitutional Court for ruling on whether it was possible to change the constitution by a referendum.
"This (possibility) is still not clear... the government will do what it has to, but it will not act against the constitution," Meciar said.

Opposition parties that did not participate in the petition, such as reformed-comunist Party of Democratic Left (SDL), have warned that the presidential referendum might open a Pandora's Box, allowing Meciar to force further single- purpose changes to the constitution by referenda.
And in his address, Meciar himself appeared ready to make his opponents words come to life.

"If we want to make an executive power independent of parliament, then we can do it also another way," Meciar said, asking, "Why only the President...why can't the Prime Minister also be elected freely by all citizens?"
